t: Minimum Non-Zero Product of the Array Elements — Push Bits to the Extremes
o: Every operation moves a single 1-bit between two numbers, so the count of ones in each bit column — and hence the total array sum — is invariant; only the distribution changes. Products shrink as numbers spread apart, so the optimum crams ones into a few huge numbers and squeezes everything else toward 1 (zero would annihilate the product, making 1 the smallest usable value). For p = 2, nums = [1, 2, 3] cannot be improved: the product stays 6. For p = 3 the extreme configuration (7, 6, 6, 6, 1, 1, 1) preserves every column count and yields 7 · 6^3 = 1512. In general keep one number at 2^p - 1, take 2^(p-1) - 1 copies of 2^p - 2 and 2^(p-1) - 1 copies of 1. Since p reaches 60, the answer must be produced with fast modular exponentiation rather than any loop over astronomically many elements.
k: Each swap relocates one 1-bit, so per-column popcounts and the total sum are invariant — reachability means same multiset of column sums.
A pair with fixed sum achieves its minimal nonzero product at the extremes, which drives all mass toward one giant number plus a sea of 1s.
The optimum is one copy of 2^p - 1 together with 2^(p-1) - 1 copies of 2^p - 2 and 2^(p-1) - 1 copies of 1, giving (2^p - 1) * (2^p - 2)^(2^(p-1) - 1).

a.n: Approach 1: Exhaustive Redistribution for Tiny p
a.i: Because reachable configurations are exactly those preserving per-column one-counts, enumerate every way to fill the 2^p - 1 slots with values whose combined bit budgets match the original array, and keep the smallest nonzero product. Only viable for p up to about 3, but it empirically confirms the closed-form formula (p = 2 gives 6, p = 3 gives 1512).
s: Compute the target one-count per bit column from the numbers 1..2^p - 1.
Recursively assign each slot a value in 1..2^p - 1 whose set bits fit the remaining budgets.
When all slots are filled and all budgets are exactly exhausted, multiply the slot values.
Track the minimum product across configurations (every value is at least 1, so products are automatically nonzero).
a.t: Exponential — roughly (2^p)^(2^p) states in the worst case; practical only for p up to 3
a.sp: O(2^p) — the slot values and bit budgets

a.n: Approach 2: Extremal Configuration with Fast Modular Power
a.i: Push redistribution to its logical end: one number absorbs every possible stray bit and becomes 2^p - 1; the remaining numbers split into 2^(p-1) - 1 copies of 2^p - 2 (all ones except the last bit) and equally many 1s. Column counts match the original array, so the configuration is reachable, and the sum-preservation plus spread-apart argument shows no nonzero product can be smaller. The product collapses to (2^p - 1) * (2^p - 2)^(2^(p-1) - 1), computed with binary exponentiation modulo 10^9 + 7; p = 1 falls out naturally as 1 * 0^0 = 1.
s: Compute top = 2^p - 1 exactly (64-bit or BigInt, since p can be 60).
Set exponent e = top >> 1, which equals 2^(p-1) - 1.
Return pow(top - 1, e, MOD) * top mod 10^9 + 7 using binary exponentiation.
a.t: O(p) — binary exponentiation performs O(p) modular multiplications on O(1)-size operands

w: Present the derivation, not just the formula: invariant column counts, spread-apart minimality, and the explicit extremal multiset. Pitfalls: computing 2^p in 32-bit arithmetic when p hits 60 (use 64-bit types or BigInt), reducing the exponent incorrectly (it is 2^(p-1) - 1, not 2^p - 2), and forgetting the product must remain nonzero so zeros are forbidden. Follow-ups: the maximum non-zero product (push numbers toward equality instead), or proving constructively that any column-count-preserving multiset is reachable via single-bit swaps.
